short_summary: Fewer than 800 patients in Scotland have received NHS weight loss injections despite official approvals, while hundreds of thousands pay privately.

image.credit: Birmingham Museums Trust, Helen Glenn, 2018-02-12 13:22:01 · CC BY 2.0

sources.name: BBC News
sources.title: Fewer than 800 Scots have received weight loss jabs on NHS, BBC finds

paragraphs: A significant healthcare disparity has emerged in Scotland, where fewer than 800 patients have received specialized weight loss injections through the National Health Service since the medications were approved years ago. While treatments such as Mounjaro and Wegovy have received official authorization for weight management, access remains severely restricted across the country's health boards. Official approvals for Mounjaro specifically for weight loss were established in Scotland in 2023, followed by Wegovy in 2024.

According to investigative findings from freedom of information requests, only six regional health bodies currently provide these GLP-1 receptor agonists specifically for weight reduction, and those programs operate strictly as small pilot projects. The health boards participating include NHS Forth Valley, NHS Borders, NHS Lothian, NHS Lanarkshire, NHS Western Isles, and the NHS State Hospital. By September 2026, a total of just 705 patients had received injections for weight loss through these initiatives. Consequently, Scotland's nine other health boards do not routinely offer the medications for obesity management, citing capacity and management challenges, though some exceptional circumstances may apply.

This limited availability stands in sharp contrast to private healthcare trends. Industry estimates from Simple Online Pharmacy suggest that at least 300,000 individuals across Scotland are currently purchasing these appetite-suppressing injections through private prescriptions. Medical professionals have voiced strong concerns regarding this growing divide, arguing that the heavy reliance on private access deepens existing health inequalities, given that obesity disproportionately affects lower-income populations.

Leading clinicians have labeled the current situation discriminatory. Dr. Mark Strachan, president of the Royal College of Physicians and a diabetes specialist, pointed out that while the NHS readily funds treatments for obesity-related complications such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, it frequently fails to provide access to interventions that address the underlying condition itself. Critics also highlight safety concerns surrounding high levels of private prescriptions that lack the comprehensive clinical support and regular multidisciplinary monitoring typically provided during formal medical oversight.

Patients like Kathleen McLaughlin, a 54-year-old from Laurieston participating in the Forth Valley pilot at Falkirk Community Hospital, emphasize the life-changing impact of structured care. Selected under strict criteria requiring a high body mass index alongside serious conditions or necessary surgery, she receives regular check-ups with a pharmacist and dietician. Having lost four stone since April, she avoided private routes due to a lack of guidance. Meanwhile, GP and health coach Dr. Jane Sehgal notes that weight management involves complex behavioral and lifestyle factors, a view echoed by private users like Sabriena Clayton who found relief through medical support.

Government officials, including Public Health Minister Maree Todd, maintain that individual health boards hold the responsibility for implementing medication availability based on phased national guidance and patient body mass index criteria, supported by the National Consensus Statement. Meanwhile, health authorities continue to evaluate how best to balance surging public demand with sustainable healthcare delivery.

facts.fact: Fewer than 800 people in Scotland have received weight loss jabs on the NHS despite approvals since 2023.
Only five or six health boards offer pilot schemes for obesity treatments, leaving nine boards without routine prescription access.
An estimated 300,000 people are accessing weight loss drugs privately in Scotland.
Medical experts describe the disparity as discriminatory and note it deepens health inequalities.
